text: Whoever isolates himself pursues his own desire; he rages against all sound judgment.
A fool takes no pleasure in understanding, but only in airing his own opinions.
When the wicked man comes, contempt comes with him, and shame brings reproach in its train.

versions.text: When the wicked man comes, contempt comes with him, and with dishonor comes disgrace.
versions.explanation: "With dishonor comes disgrace" pairs two near-synonyms in English and blurs the sense; the Hebrew pairs קָלוֹן (shame) with חֶרְפָּה (reproach). Distinguishing the two terms sharpens the parallelism and improves the spoken rhythm.

text: The words of a man's mouth are deep waters; the fountain of wisdom is a flowing stream.
It is not good to favor the wicked or to deny the righteous justice.
A fool's lips bring him into conflict, and his mouth invites a beating.
A fool's mouth is his ruin, and his lips are a snare to his soul.
The words of a gossip are like choice morsels; they go down into the innermost parts.

versions.text: The words of a gossip are like choice morsels; they sink deep into the belly.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew חַדְרֵי־בָטֶן is "the chambers of the belly," an image of the innermost self, not merely the physical stomach. "Innermost parts" keeps the metaphor of penetrating deep within a person while remaining natural for oral reading.

text: Whoever is slack in his work is brother to the one who destroys.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous one runs to it and is safe.

versions.text: The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous runs into it and is safe.
versions.explanation: "The righteous runs" mixes a collective substantive with a singular verb, which stumbles when read aloud. "The righteous one runs" preserves the singular Hebrew subject (צַדִּיק) and reads smoothly.

text: A rich man's wealth is his fortified city; in his imagination it is a towering wall.
Before destruction a man's heart is proud, but humility comes before honor.
Whoever answers before he listens—it is his folly and his shame.
A man's spirit sustains him through sickness, but a crushed spirit—who can bear it?
The discerning heart acquires knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeks it out.
A man's gift opens the way for him and brings him into the presence of great men.

versions.text: A man's gift opens the way for him and brings him before the great.
versions.explanation: "Before the great" ends the line abruptly and leaves the plural adjective without a noun, which is unclear when heard rather than read. "Great men" renders גְדֹלִים plainly and gives the clause a fuller cadence.

text: The first to plead his case seems right, until his neighbor comes and cross-examines him.
Casting lots settles disputes and keeps strong opponents apart.
A brother offended is harder to win than a fortified city, and quarrels are like the bars of a citadel.
From the fruit of his mouth a man's stomach is filled; with the harvest of his lips he is satisfied.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit.
He who finds a wife finds what is good and receives favor from the LORD.
The poor man pleads for mercy, but the rich man answers harshly.
Many companions can bring a man to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother.
